newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: NATO invitees pledge support for neighbours too.
newsitem.headline: NATO invitees pledge support for neighbours too.

text.p: Foreign ministers of the three former communist countries selected to join NATO pledged on Thursday to cooperate in preparing to enter the alliance, and to support neighbouring countries in their efforts to get in later.

After a meeting of the Czech, Hungarian, and Polish foreign ministers in Prague, host Josef Zieleniec said the governments would share information during accession talks and cooperate to convince member states to ratify the expansion.

"We agreed to show a great deal of loyalty and mutual support because the further period of our accession is certainly not a beauty contest," Hungarian foreign minister Laszlo Kovacs said at a joint news conference.
"There is no room for rivalry," he added.
The three countries were invited to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) at a summit of the alliance last week in Madrid.
NATO's current members agreed to keep the door open to future applicants fulfilling the alliance's criteria for membership after entry of the first wave of new members, expected to be in April, 1999.

The three foreign ministers made a special point of backing the efforts of Slovakia -- which was ignored in the Madrid decision because of perceived shortcomings in democratic reforms and human rights -- to achieve NATO membership.

"Openness of (NATO's) enlargement process is one of the crucial questions we discussed today," Czech minister Zieleniec said. "We agreed that the Slovak Republic is very important because all three countries neighbour (Slovakia)."

Slovakia has been sternly criticised by the United States and western European allies for what diplomats have said is a poor record in political reforms and for the government's treatment of the country's large ethnic Hungarian community.

Although Slovakia was a frontrunner for NATO membership soon after the split of Czechoslovakia in 1993, there was no reference to it in the closing Madrid communique which praised Romania, Slovenia, and the Baltic states as potential candidates.

While Zieleniec said there was an agreement among the ministers to support Slovakia's efforts for NATO membership, Hungary's foreign minister stressed that his country wanted Slovakia to meet NATO's democratic standards.

"We would like to see Slovakia maintaining its commitment to democratic values and to the Euro-Atlantic orientation in foreign policy and we want to avoid any line of division between Hungary and Slovakia," Kovacs said.
"Therefore we do support Slovakia, to meet the criteria of accession to NATO... and to be involved in the second round of enlargement."
Polish Minister Dariusz Rosati said that Slovakia's membership in the alliance was important to Poland's security.
"From the point of our national security interests it is advisable that Slovakia would be a member of the same Euro-Atlantic and European institutions," Rosati said.
